content.text:
# Paint a picture

Compose and paint one original picture in the technique of wet-on-wet
painting, at the easel, a simulator of oil paint on linen. The place,
subject and composition are yours to invent. Work from knowledge and the
notes in your studio; don't use reference images or image models.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- The easel's tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint with a rag or a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/techniques.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/wet_on_wet.md (the technique's materials and method) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed. The wet-on-wet note
describes real materials; the tubes in your box are the ones listed in
notes/easel_guide.md, and you mix your colors from them. The note's
closing section proposes how a simulator might work, but
notes/easel_guide.md describes what this easel does: the ground is dry
when painting starts, and any wet film is paint you lay over it.

After choosing a subject or technical question, use `reference` to search
the studio's reference library, or `reference_list` to browse its titles.
Read a result with `reference` by its id; follow next_page
until it is null to read the full text.

Another painter visits your studio as a critic, at the end of each sitting
and whenever you ask for a visit with `ask_critic`. The critic looks at the
painting with the same `look` you use and reads your journal and the note
you give `ask_critic` (kept in notes/to_critic.md); it doesn't paint. It
writes what it would fix and why in notes/critic.md, which you get at the
start of your next sitting or as `ask_critic`'s reply.

## Choosing the picture
Before you paint, write eight different pictures you could make from this brief in notes/concepts.md, numbered 1 to 8, each in a sentence or two. After each one, write your estimate of how many painters out of a hundred given this brief would make that picture. The studio sets aside the two with the highest estimates, rolls a die among the other six and tells you which one is yours. You make every decision from there, and the picture can develop wherever the painting takes it.

## Working
Work one campaign at a time. After laying a campaign, inspect the whole picture in normal color and relevant detail before writing the code for the next campaign. Let what you see inform the next action; record what changes or why continuing unchanged serves the picture.

After the first large masses, consider whether the whole picture produces your intended effect: how its large shapes, values and spatial relationships support it, and whether anything weakens it. Improve a weakening relationship in the large masses, or deliberately accept it with your reason, before you build detail over them. After a local repair, check its effect on the whole picture. If the repair recreates the problem, reconsider the composition or method before expanding it.

Before repeating an unfamiliar mixture or stroke, inspect a small trial, on the scratch canvas beside the painting (`scratch: true`) or on the painting, laid on the intended substrate after the intended treatment, alongside the existing marks in a detail crop. A held pile shows thick paint on steel; use the laid trial to judge its effect on the picture. For material trials and repairs, keep useful observations in your journal: substrate and wetness, recipe ratios, medium or thinner, brush load, coverage and the viewed result. Carry forward the conditions that mattered and label broader rules as hypotheses until a further trial isolates them.

- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,
  change approach and discover where the painting can go.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages.
- An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
  one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
- Your journal handoff at the end of each sitting lists the passages
  still open under a line reading `Open passages:`, or reads
  `Open passages: none` when nothing is open, and the next sitting opens
  with that list. The painting is finished when you end a sitting in
  which you made no marks on the painting and looked at the whole canvas
  and at a detail crop in normal color, even if the list still names
  passages. Record your reflections in your journal before you end that
  sitting.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

content.text:
# Wet-on-wet landscape painting: materials and technique for an oil-paint simulator

**Scope.** This note covers the fast alla prima landscape method, where a whole landscape is finished in one sitting and every layer goes into wet paint. It describes the ground, paint, tools, order of work and the physics that makes it hold together. Values tagged **[est]** are engineering guesses to tune, not measured figures.

---

## 1. Ground

- **Support:** a stretched, double-primed canvas, commonly 18×24 in (457×610 mm). The priming makes it nonabsorbent, so the wet ground stays open and the weave stands up through it.
- **Variants:** a black or gray gesso ground, left to dry fully, for night scenes and strong contrast. Contact paper or tape can mask a shape (an oval, a window) before the ground goes on, which gives a vignette with a clean edge.
- **Liquid white:** an oil white thinned with oil and a little solvent. One manufacturer's safety data sheet gives 1–10% hydrotreated heavy naphtha, density 1.2–1.6 g/cm³ and a flash point near 62 °C; the full recipe is unpublished. A home version of about one part titanium white to one part linseed oil is common but unverified. A liquid black (the same medium with carbon black) serves dark grounds, and a pigment-free liquid clear keeps the slip without lightening the colors laid into it.
- **Application:** a thin, even coat over the whole canvas with a wide flat brush, just enough to cover it. Painting starts while it is still wet. No thickness figure is published.
- **What it does:** colors laid into the wet ground slide and blend on the canvas, and brushing across it removes excess paint, so later layers go on easily. Each stroke also picks up some of the white, so color laid into liquid white comes out lighter. That is why the clear version exists.

## 2. Paint

**Palette.** A small fixed set of firm oils: titanium white, phthalo blue, prussian blue, phthalo green, alizarin crimson, a bright red, a cadmium-yellow hue, indian yellow, yellow ochre, sap green, dark sienna, van dyke brown, a chromatic black and a premixed mountain dark.

| Color | CI pigments | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Titanium white | PW6 | opaque |
| Phthalo blue | PB15:3 | very strong; it overwhelms crimson in a mix |
| Prussian blue | PB27 (some labels add PG178, PB198; **conflict**) |  |
| Phthalo green | PG7 |  |
| Alizarin crimson | PR83 | transparent |
| Bright red | PR255, PR254 | not cadmium |
| Cadmium yellow hue | PY74 | not cadmium |
| Indian yellow | PY83 |  |
| Yellow ochre | PY43 |  |
| Sap green | PY42, PY83, PG7 |  |
| Dark sienna | PBr7 |  |
| Van dyke brown | PBr7, PBk9 |  |
| Chromatic black | PR83, PG7 | a deep green-crimson, not a neutral black |
| Mountain dark | PB27, PBr7, PBk9, PR83, PG7 | premixed |

**Consistency:** the paint is far stiffer than ordinary tube oil, close to dry, and that firmness is what makes the method work. No viscosity or yield data are published.

**Thinning:** thinner goes on sparingly, a touch on the brush so the new paint is a little softer than the paint already on the canvas. Liner paint is thinned until it almost runs. The thinner is an odorless hydrocarbon solvent with kinematic viscosity at or below about 20 mm²/s.

## 3. Tools

The landscape brushes mix natural and synthetic bristle; the liner and the soft blender are natural bristle.

| Tool | Size and use and handling |
| --- | --- |
| **2-inch flat** | head ≈50 mm wide, hair ≈63 mm long. Skies, water and any large area. Loaded by tapping into the paint so only the top bristles carry it. Clouds: dab with one corner, then small circles with the brush on its side. Mist: tap the base of a shape with a clean, dry brush and lift gently upward. A brush wet with thinner thins the paint and turns it mushy. |
| **1-inch flat** | 25 mm. Base coats for clouds, water, mountains, trees and bushes; crisscross strokes at mountain bases for fog. |
| **1-inch oval** | Evergreens, foothills and highlights. |
| **#6 fan** | [est] 30–35 mm. Evergreens (heavily loaded on both sides), distant trees (the top corner only), grass (long flat strokes pushed upward, back and forth in a zigzag), trunks, foothills, boats. |
| **#3 fan** | [est] ~20 mm. The same marks, smaller and tighter. |
| **#6 filbert** | Trunks, waves and detail. |
| **Liner** | point [est] 1–2 mm. Loaded with thin paint, the bristles rolled to a sharp point. Twigs, fine branches and the signature. |
| **#10 knife** | straight blade ≈95×32 mm. Larger and stiffer than an ordinary painting knife, with a straight edge. Mountains. |
| **#5 knife** | smaller. Tight areas. |

**Knife loading:** paint is pressed out flat on the palette, then the knife edge cuts across it and picks up a thin bead of paint along the edge.

**Knife deposit:**
- **Mountain body:** the dark goes on firmly and the excess is scraped back, but not all of it. Scraping too much leaves too little dark for the highlights to read against.
- **Highlights:** almost no pressure. The bead glides over the dark and breaks on the texture, leaving gaps, and the gaps are what make it read as rock. Solid, even coverage looks like frosting.
- **Direction:** highlight and shadow strokes follow the slope of each face.
- **Scratching:** the knife point scratches in sticks and twigs.

**Cleaning:** the brush is washed in odorless thinner, then the excess is shaken and knocked out against something hard, so it goes back to the paint nearly dry.

## 4. Order of work

A winter lake scene shows the usual sequence:

1. Liquid white over the whole canvas with the 2-inch brush, left wet.
2. Sky: alizarin crimson crisscrossed low for a glow. Phthalo blue with the chromatic black above, crisscrossed all the way across the top, then blended downward without overworking.
3. Water: the same colors in horizontal strokes.
4. Mountain: the knife with a dark mix (prussian blue, chromatic black, van dyke brown, alizarin). The body is softened with the 1-inch brush and its base crisscrossed into fog.
5. Mountain highlights: a small bead of white on the lit side; white, phthalo blue and a little of the dark on the shadow side. Tap the base and lift for mist.
6. Background evergreens: the mountain dark plus a little white, on the fan brush.
7. Reflections: the 1-inch brush pulled straight down (an angled pull makes them look wrong), then light horizontal passes across. The water line: a very small bead of titanium white mixed with liquid white, cut in with the knife.
8. Foreground evergreens and bushes pushed up in dark. Scratched twigs.
9. Highlights: white, liquid white and a touch of blue, leaving some dark showing. Wipe the brush whenever it picks up dark.
10. Liner work and the signature.


[71 more lines in file. Use offset=81 to continue.]

content.thinking:
I'm brainstorming classic Bob Ross wet-on-wet subjects—mountain lakes with evergreens and reflections, winter cabins, seascapes, sunset lakes—and trying to estimate how common each concept would be among a hundred painters attempting this style, since the two most popular get set aside for honesty's sake.

I'm also sketching out more unusual options to diversify the set: a vignette night marsh scene, a desert mesa, a still life pail of flowers, foggy farmland, a harbor at dawn, rainy city streets, or a prairie grain elevator under storm clouds, before settling on eight final concepts with rough percentage estimates for each.

Estimate 1. The totals don't need to add to exactly 100, just roughly proportional, so I'll move on to writing the file.

arguments.text:
1. A snow-capped mountain range above a still alpine lake, with evergreens on both shores, mirrored reflections pulled straight down, and soft fog at the mountain's base.
Estimate: 38/100

2. A log cabin in snowy woods at sunset. A warm light shows in the window, a trodden path leads in, and bare trees stand dark against a crimson and gold sky.
Estimate: 14/100

3. An ocean wave breaking at sunset, with light shining through its green curl, foam spilling down the face, and a dark rocky headland at one side.
Estimate: 9/100

4. An autumn woodland stream falling over mossy rocks in a small waterfall, with white birches and gold and rust foliage reflected in the pool below.
Estimate: 7/100

5. A moonlit marsh on a black ground, framed in an oval vignette: cattails and reeds in silhouette, and a silver path of moonlight across the open water.
Estimate: 4/100

6. A prairie thunderstorm: a towering anvil cloud over a wheat field, with a lone grain elevator caught in a last shaft of low sun and gray rain curtains trailing at the horizon.
Estimate: 3/100

7. A small fishing harbor at dawn in thick fog. Old pilings and two moored dories sit in the foreground, and the far wharf and boats dissolve into pearl gray.
Estimate: 3/100

8. A rainy city street at dusk seen from a cafe window, with wet pavement holding long reflections of shop signs, headlights and a red bus.
Estimate: 1/100

content.text:
I've saved eight picture ideas with estimates to notes/concepts.md. I didn't paint or title anything, since this sitting was only for the concepts.

Most painters given this brief would probably make the standard alpine-lake scene, so I gave it the highest estimate (38/100). The snowy cabin at sunset came next (14/100). Those are the two the studio sets aside.

The other six, in falling order of likelihood, are:
- a breaking ocean wave at sunset
- an autumn stream with a small waterfall
- a moonlit marsh in an oval on a black ground
- a prairie thunderstorm with a lone grain elevator
- a fishing harbor at dawn in fog
- a rainy city street seen from a cafe window, which is the least likely (1/100)

I'll wait for the die roll.
